title: Mastery Challenge: Film & TV
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Film & TV Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from across the tree: early film, silent film, shooting, cutting, studios, genres, world cinema, TV, blockbusters and effects, critical watching. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Film & TV Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the whole tree, from the first flickering frames to reading a film critically. Level 1 showed you that a movie is still pictures shown fast; now see how much you can read in them. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Film & TV: mastered
learned: How still frames, cuts, sound and color work together to steer what an audience feels and believes.
How silent pioneers, the studios, genres and filmmakers around the world shaped what cinema became.
How television grew out of radio, and why cable and streaming split its audience.
What blockbusters, home video and effects from matte paintings to computers changed about which films got made.

questions.prompt: Put these milestones from across the tree in order, from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: The Lumières' paid screening was in 1895, The Jazz Singer came in 1927, I Love Lucy debuted in 1951, Toy Story arrived in 1995 and House of Cards in 2013.

questions.prompt: What were the bent, out-of-proportion sets of The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari designed to show?

options.label: The studio couldn't afford proper carpenters
options.rationale: The distortion was deliberate design.

options.label: To show a narrator's tortured state of mind
To hide the camera crew
options.rationale: The sets were designed to express a mind.

options.label: Because the film was shot outdoors
options.rationale: It was shot on designed sets.

questions.explanation: Wiene hired Expressionist artists to build deformed sets that show the narrator's tortured mind.

questions.prompt: A director wants a villain to loom over the audience. Where should the camera go?

options.label: Below eye level, looking up
Above the villain, looking down
options.rationale: A high angle makes characters look small.

options.label: Exactly at eye level
options.rationale: That's the neutral, standard angle.

options.label: Behind the villain's head
options.rationale: That isn't about looming.

questions.explanation: A low angle looks up at a character and can make a villain scary and intimidating.

questions.prompt: By Kuleshov's experiment, an actor's neutral face cut next to a bowl of soup will seem to show _____.

options.label: no emotion at all
options.rationale: Viewers read emotion into the face.

options.label: grief
options.rationale: That came from the corpse shot.

options.label: hunger
tenderness
options.rationale: That came from the child shot.

questions.explanation: Viewers read the same face as hungry, tender or grieving depending on the shot beside it.

questions.prompt: What did Gregg Toland's deep focus let Citizen Kane's audiences do?

options.label: See the film in color
options.rationale: Kane is black and white.

options.label: Hear the actors more clearly
options.rationale: Deep focus is about the image.

options.label: Watch it on a wide, curved screen with three projectors
options.rationale: That's Cinerama, a different change.

options.label: See sharp detail near and far, and choose where to look

questions.explanation: Characters and objects were sharp in all parts of the screen in nearly every scene.

questions.prompt: What turns Hitchcock's bomb scene from 15 seconds of surprise into 15 minutes of suspense?

options.label: Letting the audience see the bomb and the clock
Making the bomb bigger
options.rationale: Size doesn't create suspense; knowledge does.

options.label: Cutting the scene faster
options.rationale: The key is what the audience knows.

options.label: Removing the bomb entirely
options.rationale: Then there's nothing to fear.

questions.explanation: Show the bomb planted and the clock ticking, and the audience participates in the scene.

questions.prompt: What makes Kurosawa's Rashomon an unusual kind of story?

options.label: It has no dialogue
options.rationale: It is a sound film with dialogue.

options.label: One crime is recalled in four conflicting versions
It was filmed in a single unbroken take with no cuts
options.rationale: Its structure, not its takes, is the point.

options.label: It was the first film in color
options.rationale: It's black and white.

questions.explanation: A samurai, his wife, a bandit and a woodcutter each recall the same crime differently.

questions.prompt: Most early 1950s shows reached the West Coast as kinescopes. Why did I Love Lucy's makers shoot on film instead?

options.label: Film let the show go out live in every time zone
options.rationale: Film had to be developed first; it was never live.

options.label: Film let them skip editing the three cameras
options.rationale: Three streams of film still had to be cut together.

options.label: Film was cheaper, because each roll was reused
options.rationale: The payoff came from reusing the finished episodes, not the raw film.

options.label: A sharp picture everywhere, and reruns for years

questions.explanation: Kinescopes looked like TV seen through cheesecloth. A filmed show looked sharp in every time zone, and in 1955 I Love Lucy became one of the first series broadcast as reruns.

questions.prompt: Hollywood first fought television, and later fought the VCR. What did the VCR turn into for the studios?

options.label: A big source of income, through tape rentals
A tool the studios got banned in court
options.rationale: Universal lost: the Court ruled 5 to 4 that selling VCRs was legal.

options.label: A way to show films in theaters without prints
options.rationale: Tapes were for watching at home.

options.label: A cheaper camera format for shooting features
options.rationale: The VCR recorded and played tapes at home; it didn't shoot films.

questions.explanation: Studios resisted the VCR as they had resisted TV, but by 1983 most sold tapes to rental stores and home users, and rentals soon made up a significant share of a film's revenue.

questions.prompt: Why is 'red means passion' a weak rule for reading films?

options.label: Films never use red
options.rationale: Many do, with different meanings.

options.label: Red always means danger on screen, never passion, love or anything else
options.rationale: No color has a fixed meaning.

options.label: The same color can mean passion in one film and decay in another
Only grading can make red
options.rationale: Color is chosen in many ways.

questions.explanation: Ju Dou uses red for passion, Cries and Whispers for stagnation: read color in context.
